title="Tel Aviv University">Tel Aviv University</a>), mathematics (<a href="/wiki/Hebrew_University_of_Jerusalem" title="Hebrew University of Jerusalem">Hebrew University of Jerusalem</a>) and chemistry (<a href="/wiki/Weizmann_Institute_of_Science" title="Weizmann Institute of Science">Weizmann Institute of Science</a>).<sup id="cite_ref-ARWU_393-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-ARWU-393">&#91;386&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>In 2012, Israel was ranked ninth in the world by the Futron's <a href="/wiki/Space_Competitiveness_Index" title="Space Competitiveness Index">Space Competitiveness Index</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-600" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-600">&#91;593&#93;</a></sup> The <a href="/wiki/Israel_Space_Agency" title="Israel Space Agency">Israel Space Agency</a> coordinates all Israeli space research programmes with scientific and commercial goals, and have indigenously designed and built at least 13 commercial, research and spy satellites.<sup id="cite_ref-601" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-601">&#91;594&#93;</a></sup> Some of Israel's satellites are ranked among the world's most advanced space systems.<sup id="cite_ref-602" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-602">&#91;595&#93;</a></sup> <a href="/wiki/Shavit_2" title="Shavit 2">Shavit</a> is a space <a href="/wiki/Launch_vehicle" title="Launch vehicle">launch vehicle</a> produced by Israel to launch small <a href="/wiki/Satellite" title="Satellite">satellites</a> into <a href="/wiki/Low_Earth_orbit" title="Low Earth orbit">low Earth orbit</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-603" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-603">&#91;596&#93;</a></sup> It was first launched in 1988, making Israel the <a href="/wiki/Timeline_of_first_orbital_launches_by_country" title="Timeline of first orbital launches by country">eighth nation</a> to have a space launch capability. In 2003, <a href="/wiki/Ilan_Ramon" title="Ilan Ramon">Ilan Ramon</a> became Israel's first astronaut, serving as payload specialist of <a href="/wiki/STS-107" title="STS-107">STS-107</a>, the <a href="/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Columbia_disaster" title="Space Shuttle Columbia disaster">fatal mission</a> of the <a href="/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Columbia" title="Space Shuttle Columbia">Space Shuttle <i>Columbia</i></a>.<sup id="cite_ref-604" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-604">&#91;597&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>The ongoing shortage of <a href="/wiki/Water_supply_and_sanitation_in_Israel" title="Water supply and sanitation in Israel">water in the country</a> has spurred innovation in <a href="/wiki/Water_conservation" title="Water conservation">water conservation</a> techniques, and a substantial <a href="/wiki/Agricultural_research_in_Israel" title="Agricultural research in Israel">agricultural modernization</a>, <a href="/wiki/Drip_irrigation" title="Drip irrigation">drip irrigation</a>, was <a href="/wiki/List_of_Israeli_inventions_and_discoveries" title="List of Israeli inventions and discoveries">invented in Israel</a>. Israel is also at the technological forefront of <a href="/wiki/Desalination" title="Desalination">desalination</a> and <a href="/wiki/Water_recycling" class="mw-redirect" title="Water recycling">water recycling</a>. The <a href="/wiki/Sorek_desalination_plant" class="mw-redirect" title="Sorek desalination plant">Sorek desalination plant</a> is the largest seawater <a href="/wiki/Reverse_osmosis" title="Reverse osmosis">reverse osmosis</a> (SWRO) <a href="/wiki/Desalination_facilities" class="mw-redirect" title="Desalination facilities">desalination facility</a> in the world.<sup id="cite_ref-605" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-605">&#91;598&#93;</a></sup> By 2014, Israel's desalination programmes provided roughly 35% of Israel's drinking water and it is expected to supply 40% by 2015 and 70% by 2050.<sup id="cite_ref-606" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-606">&#91;599&#93;</a></sup> As of 2015<sup class="plainlinks noexcerpt noprint asof-tag update" style="display:none;"><a class="external text" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Israel&amp;action=edit">&#91;update&#93;</a></sup>, more than 50 percent of the water for Israeli households, agriculture and industry is artificially produced.<sup id="cite_ref-Kershner_607-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Kershner-607">&#91;600&#93;</a></sup> The country hosts an annual Water Technology and Environmental Control Exhibition &amp; Conference (WATEC) that attracts thousands of people from across the world.<sup id="cite_ref-608" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-608">&#91;601&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-609" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-609">&#91;602&#93;</a></sup> In 2011, Israel's <a href="/wiki/Water_industry" title="Water industry">water technology industry</a> was worth around $2 billion a year with annual exports of products and services in the tens of millions of dollars. As a result of innovations in reverse osmosis technology, Israel is set to become a net <a href="/wiki/Water_export" title="Water export">exporter of water</a> in the coming years.<sup id="cite_ref-610" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-610">&#91;603&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Solar_dish_at_Ben-Gurion_National_Solar_Energy_Center_in_Israel.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img alt="A horizontal parabolic dish, with a triangular structure on its top." src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/24/Solar_dish_at_Ben-Gurion_National_Solar_Energy_Center_in_Israel.jpg/220px-Solar_dish_at_Ben-Gurion_National_Solar_Energy_Center_in_Israel.jpg" decoding="async" width="220" height="165" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/24/Solar_dish_at_Ben-Gurion_National_Solar_Energy_Center_in_Israel.jpg/330px-Solar_dish_at_Ben-Gurion_National_Solar_Energy_Center_in_Israel.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/24/Solar_dish_at_Ben-Gurion_National_Solar_Energy_Center_in_Israel.jpg/440px-Solar_dish_at_Ben-Gurion_National_Solar_Energy_Center_in_Israel.jpg 2x" data-file-width="3340" data-file-height="2504" /></a><figcaption>The world's largest <a href="/wiki/Parabolic_reflector" title="Parabolic reflector">solar parabolic dish</a> at the <a href="/wiki/Ben-Gurion_National_Solar_Energy_Center" title="Ben-Gurion National Solar Energy Center">Ben-Gurion National Solar Energy Center</a><sup id="cite_ref-Register_611-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Register-611">&#91;604&#93;</a></sup></figcaption></figure>
<p>Israel has embraced <a href="/wiki/Solar_power_in_Israel" title="Solar power in Israel">solar energy</a>; its engineers are on the cutting edge of solar energy technology<sup id="cite_ref-NPR_612-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-NPR-612">&#91;605&#93;</a></sup> and its solar companies work on projects around the world.<sup id="cite_ref-CBC_613-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-CBC-613">&#91;606&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-BW_614-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-BW-614">&#91;607&#93;</a></sup> Over 90% of Israeli homes use solar energy for hot water, the highest per capita in the world.<sup id="cite_ref-Solar_energy_299-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Solar_energy-299">&#91;292&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-Environment_California_SWH_615-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Environment_California_SWH-615">&#91;608&#93;</a></sup> According to government figures, the country saves 8% of its electricity consumption per year because of its solar energy use in heating.<sup id="cite_ref-616" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-616">&#91;609&#93;</a></sup> The high annual incident <a href="/wiki/Irradiance" title="Irradiance">solar irradiance</a> at its geographic <a href="/wiki/Latitude" title="Latitude">latitude</a> creates ideal conditions for what is an internationally renowned solar research and development industry in the <a href="/wiki/Negev_Desert" class="mw-redirect" title="Negev Desert">Negev Desert</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-NPR_612-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-NPR-612">&#91;605&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-CBC_613-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-CBC-613">&#91;606&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-BW_614-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-BW-614">&#91;607&#93;</a></sup> Israel had a modern <a href="/wiki/Electric_vehicle_network" class="mw-redirect" title="Electric vehicle network">electric car infrastructure</a> involving a countrywide network of <a href="/wiki/Charging_station" title="Charging station">charging stations</a> to facilitate the charging and exchange of car batteries. It was thought that this would have lowered Israel's oil dependency and lowered the fuel costs of hundreds of Israel's motorists that use cars powered only by electric batteries.<sup id="cite_ref-617" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-617">&#91;610&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-618" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-618">&#91;611&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-619" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-619">&#91;612&#93;</a></sup> The Israeli model was being studied by several countries and being implemented in Denmark and Australia.<sup id="cite_ref-620" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-620">&#91;613&#93;</a></sup> However, Israel's trailblazing electric car company <a href="/wiki/Better_Place_(company)" title="Better Place (company)">Better Place</a> shut down in 2013.<sup id="cite_ref-621" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-621">&#91;614&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h3><span class="mw-headline" id="Energy">Energy</span></h3>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main article: <a href="/wiki/Energy_in_Israel" title="Energy in Israel">Energy in Israel</a></div>
<p>Israel began producing natural gas from its own offshore gas fields in 2004. Between 2005 and 2012, Israel had imported gas from Egypt via the al-<a href="/wiki/Arish%E2%80%93Ashkelon_pipeline" class="mw-redirect" title="Arish–Ashkelon pipeline">Arish–Ashkelon pipeline</a>, which was terminated due to <a href="/wiki/Egyptian_crisis_(2011%E2%80%9314)" class="mw-redirect" title="Egyptian crisis (2011–14)">Egyptian Crisis of 2011–14</a>. In 2009, a <a href="/wiki/Natural_gas_in_Israel" title="Natural gas in Israel">natural gas</a> reserve, <a href="/wiki/Tamar_gas_field" title="Tamar gas field">Tamar</a>, was found near the coast of Israel. A second natural gas reserve, <a href="/wiki/Leviathan_gas_field" title="Leviathan gas field">Leviathan</a>, was discovered in 2010.<sup id="cite_ref-622" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-622">&#91;615&#93;</a></sup> The natural gas reserves in these two fields (Leviathan has around 19 trillion cubic feet) could make Israel energy secure for more than 50 years. In 2013, Israel began commercial production of natural gas from the Tamar field. As of 2014<sup class="plainlinks noexcerpt noprint asof-tag update" style="display:none;"><a class="external text" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Israel&amp;action=edit">&#91;update&#93;</a></sup>, Israel produced over 7.5 billion cubic meters (bcm) of <a href="/wiki/Natural_gas" title="Natural gas">natural gas</a> a year.<sup id="cite_ref-623" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-623">&#91;616&#93;</a></sup> Israel had 199 billion cubic meters (bcm) of proven reserves of natural gas as of the start of 2016.<sup id="cite_ref-624" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-624">&#91;617&#93;</a></sup> The Leviathan gas field started production in 2019.<sup id="cite_ref-625" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-625">&#91;618&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p><a href="/wiki/Ketura_Sun" title="Ketura Sun">Ketura Sun</a> is Israel's first commercial solar field. Built in early 2011 by the <a href="/wiki/Arava_Power_Company" title="Arava Power Company">Arava Power Company</a> on <a href="/wiki/Ketura,_Israel" title="Ketura, Israel">Kibbutz Ketura</a>, Ketura Sun covers twenty acres and is expected to produce green energy amounting to 4.95 <a href="/wiki/Megawatts" class="mw-redirect" title="Megawatts">megawatts</a> (MW). The field consists of 18,500 <a href="/wiki/Photovoltaics" title="Photovoltaics">photovoltaic</a> panels made by <a href="/wiki/Suntech_Power" title="Suntech Power">Suntech</a>, which will produce about 9 <a href="/wiki/Gigawatt-hour" class="mw-redirect" title="Gigawatt-hour">gigawatt-hours</a> (GWh) of electricity per year.<sup id="cite_ref-626" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-626">&#91;619&#93;</a></sup> In the next twenty years, the field will spare the production of some 125,000 metric tons of carbon dioxide.<sup id="cite_ref-627" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-627">&#91;620&#93;</a></sup> The field was inaugurated on 15 June 2011.<sup id="cite_ref-628" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-628">&#91;621&#93;</a></sup> On 22 May 2012 <a href="/wiki/Arava_Power_Company" title="Arava Power Company">Arava Power Company</a> announced that it had reached financial close on an additional 58.5 MW for 8 projects to be built in the Arava and the Negev valued at 780 million NIS or approximately $204 million.<sup id="cite_ref-629" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-629">&#91;622&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h3><span class="mw-headline" id="Transport">Transport</span></h3>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main article: <a href="/wiki/Transport_in_Israel" title="Transport in Israel">Transport in Israel</a></div>
<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:4X-ECC_LLBG_09-05-2014b.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/7b/4X-ECC_LLBG_09-05-2014b.jpg/220px-4X-ECC_LLBG_09-05-2014b.jpg" decoding="async" width="220" height="165" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/7b/4X-ECC_LLBG_09-05-2014b.jpg/330px-4X-ECC_LLBG_09-05-2014b.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/7b/4X-ECC_LLBG_09-05-2014b.jpg/440px-4X-ECC_LLBG_09-05-2014b.jpg 2x" data-file-width="4160" data-file-height="3113" /></a><figcaption><a href="/wiki/Ben_Gurion_International_Airport" class="mw-redirect" title="Ben Gurion International Airport">Ben Gurion International Airport</a></figcaption></figure>
<p>Israel has a modern transport system. The country has 19,224 kilometres (11,945&#160;mi) of paved <a href="/wiki/Roads_in_Israel" title="Roads in Israel">roads</a>,<sup id="cite_ref-630" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-630">&#91;623&#93;</a></sup> and 3&#160;million motor vehicles.<sup id="cite_ref-vehicles_631-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-vehicles-631">&#91;624&#93;</a></sup> The <a href="/wiki/List_of_countries_by_vehicles_per_capita" title="List of countries by vehicles per capita">number of motor vehicles per 1,000 persons</a> is 365, relatively low with respect to developed countries.<sup id="cite_ref-vehicles_631-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-vehicles-631">&#91;624&#93;</a></sup> Israel has 5,715 buses on scheduled routes,<sup id="cite_ref-632" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-632">&#91;625&#93;</a></sup> operated by several carriers, the largest and oldest of which is <a href="/wiki/Egged_(company)" title="Egged (company)">Egged</a>, serving most of the country.<sup id="cite_ref-633" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-633">&#91;626&#93;</a></sup> <a href="/wiki/Rail_transport_in_Israel" title="Rail transport in Israel">Railways</a> stretch across 1,277 kilometres (793&#160;mi) and are operated solely by government-owned <a href="/wiki/Israel_Railways" title="Israel Railways">Israel Railways</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-cbs_rails_634-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-cbs_rails-634">&#91;627&#93;</a></sup> Following major investments beginning in the early to mid-1990s, the number of train passengers per year has grown from 2.5&#160;million in 1990, to 53&#160;million in 2015; railways are also transporting 7.5&#160;million tons of cargo, per year.<sup id="cite_ref-cbs_rails_634-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-cbs_rails-634">&#91;627&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Israel is served by three international <a href="/wiki/List_of_airports_in_Israel" title="List of airports in Israel">airports</a>, <a href="/wiki/Ben_Gurion_Airport" title="Ben Gurion Airport">Ben Gurion Airport</a>, the country's main hub for international air travel near Tel Aviv, <a href="/wiki/Ramon_Airport" title="Ramon Airport">Ramon Airport</a>, which serves the southernmost port city of Eilat and <a href="/wiki/Haifa_Airport" title="Haifa Airport">Haifa Airport</a> in the North of the country. Ben Gurion, Israel's largest airport, handled over 15&#160;million passengers in 2015.<sup id="cite_ref-635" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-635">&#91;628&#93;</a></sup> The country has three main ports: the <a href="/wiki/Port_of_Haifa" title="Port of Haifa">Port of Haifa</a>, the country's oldest and largest, on the <a href="/wiki/Mediterranean" class="mw-redirect" title="Mediterranean">Mediterranean</a> coast, <a href="/wiki/Ashdod_Port" class="mw-redirect" title="Ashdod Port">Ashdod Port</a>; and the smaller <a href="/wiki/Port_of_Eilat" title="Port of Eilat">Port of Eilat</a> on the <a href="/wiki/Red_Sea" title="Red Sea">Red Sea</a>.
</p>
<h3><span class="mw-headline" id="Tourism">Tourism</span></h3>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main article: <a href="/wiki/Tourism_in_Israel" title="Tourism in Israel">Tourism in Israel</a></div>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">See also: <a href="/wiki/List_of_archaeological_sites_in_Israel_and_Palestine" title="List of archaeological sites in Israel and Palestine">List of archaeological sites in Israel and Palestine</a></div>
<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Ein_Bokek_-_Dead_Sea2.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f3/Ein_Bokek_-_Dead_Sea2.jpg/220px-Ein_Bokek_-_Dead_Sea2.jpg" decoding="async" width="220" height="148" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f3/Ein_Bokek_-_Dead_Sea2.jpg/330px-Ein_Bokek_-_Dead_Sea2.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f3/Ein_Bokek_-_Dead_Sea2.jpg/440px-Ein_Bokek_-_Dead_Sea2.jpg 2x" data-file-width="5288" data-file-height="3552" /></a><figcaption><a href="/wiki/Ein_Bokek" title="Ein Bokek">Ein Bokek</a> resort on the shore of the <a href="/wiki/Dead_Sea" title="Dead Sea">Dead Sea</a></figcaption></figure>
<p>Tourism, especially <a href="/wiki/Religious_tourism" title="Religious tourism">religious tourism</a>, is an important industry in Israel, with the country's temperate climate, <a href="/wiki/List_of_beaches_in_Israel" title="List of beaches in Israel">beaches</a>, <a href="/wiki/Archaeology_of_Israel" title="Archaeology of Israel">archaeological</a>, other <a href="/wiki/List_of_World_Heritage_Sites_in_Israel" title="List of World Heritage Sites in Israel">historical</a> and <a href="/wiki/List_of_biblical_places" title="List of biblical places">biblical</a> sites, and unique geography also drawing tourists. Israel's security problems have taken their toll on the industry, but the number of incoming tourists is on the rebound.<sup id="cite_ref-636" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-636">&#91;629&#93;</a></sup> In 2017, a record of 3.6 million tourists visited Israel, yielding a 25 percent growth since 2016 and contributed NIS 20 billion to the Israeli economy.<sup id="cite_ref-637" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-637">&#91;630&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-638" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-638">&#91;631&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-639" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-639">&#91;632&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-640" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-640">&#91;633&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h3><span class="mw-headline" id="Real_estate">Real estate</span></h3>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main article: <a href="/wiki/Housing_in_Israel" title="Housing in Israel">Housing in Israel</a></div>
<p>Housing prices in Israel are listed in the top third,<sup id="cite_ref-641" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-641">&#91;634&#93;</a></sup> with an average of 150 salaries required to buy an apartment.<sup id="cite_ref-642" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-642">&#91;635&#93;</a></sup> As of 2022, there are about 2.7 million properties in Israel, with an annual increase of more than 50,000.<sup id="cite_ref-643" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-643">&#91;636&#93;</a></sup> However, the demand for housing exceeds supply, with a shortage of about 200,000 apartments as of 2021,<sup id="cite_ref-644" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-644">&#91;637&#93;</a></sup> and thus rising house prices. As a result, by 2021 housing prices rose by 5.6%.<sup id="cite_ref-645" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-645">&#91;638&#93;</a></sup> High prices do not stop Israelis from buying properties. In 2021, Israelis took a record of NIS 116.1 billion in mortgages, an increase of 50% from 2020.<sup id="cite_ref-646" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-646">&#91;639&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h2><span class="mw-headline" id="Culture">Culture</span></h2>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main article: <a href="/wiki/Culture_of_Israel" title="Culture of Israel">Culture of Israel</a></div>
<p>Israel's diverse culture stems from the diversity of its population. Jews from diaspora communities around the world brought their cultural and religious traditions back with them, creating a melting pot of Jewish customs and beliefs.<sup id="cite_ref-647" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-647">&#91;640&#93;</a></sup> Arab influences are present in many cultural spheres,<sup id="cite_ref-MendelRanta2016p137_648-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-MendelRanta2016p137-648">&#91;641&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-MendelRanta2016p140_649-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-MendelRanta2016p140-649">&#91;642&#93;</a></sup> such as <a href="/wiki/Architecture_of_Israel" title="Architecture of Israel">architecture</a>,<sup id="cite_ref-650" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-650">&#91;643&#93;</a></sup> <a href="/wiki/Music_of_Israel" title="Music of Israel">music</a>,<sup id="cite_ref-651" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-651">&#91;644&#93;</a></sup> and <a href="/wiki/Israeli_cuisine" title="Israeli cuisine">cuisine</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-652" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-652">&#91;645&#93;</a></sup> Israel is the only country in the world where life revolves around the <a href="/wiki/Hebrew_calendar" title="Hebrew calendar">Hebrew calendar</a>. <a href="/wiki/Public_holidays_in_Israel" title="Public holidays in Israel">Work and school holidays</a> are determined by the <a href="/wiki/Jewish_holiday" class="mw-redirect" title="Jewish holiday">Jewish holidays</a>, and the official day of rest is Saturday, the <a href="/wiki/Shabbat" title="Shabbat">Jewish Sabbath</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-653" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-653">&#91;646&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h3><span class="mw-headline" id="Literature">Literature</span></h3>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main article: <a href="/wiki/Israeli_literature" title="Israeli literature">Israeli literature</a></div>
<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Agnon.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/cd/Agnon.jpg/170px-Agnon.jpg" decoding="async" width="170" height="227" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/cd/Agnon.jpg/255px-Agnon.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/cd/Agnon.jpg/340px-Agnon.jpg 2x" data-file-width="651" data-file-height="868" /></a><figcaption><a href="/wiki/Shmuel_Yosef_Agnon" title="Shmuel Yosef Agnon">Shmuel Yosef Agnon</a>, laureate of the <a href="/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Literature" title="Nobel Prize in Literature">Nobel Prize in Literature</a></figcaption></figure>
<p><a href="/wiki/Israeli_literature" title="Israeli literature">Israeli literature</a> is primarily <a href="/wiki/Modern_Hebrew_poetry" title="Modern Hebrew poetry">poetry</a> and prose written in <a href="/wiki/Hebrew_language" title="Hebrew language">Hebrew</a>, as part of the <a href="/wiki/Revival_of_the_Hebrew_language" title="Revival of the Hebrew language">renaissance</a> of Hebrew as a spoken language since the mid-19th century, although a small body of literature is published in other languages, such as English. By law, two copies of all printed matter published in Israel must be deposited in the <a href="/wiki/National_Library_of_Israel" title="National Library of Israel">National Library of Israel</a> at the <a href="/wiki/Hebrew_University_of_Jerusalem" title="Hebrew University of Jerusalem">Hebrew University of Jerusalem</a>. In 2001, the law was amended to include audio and video recordings, and other non-print media.<sup id="cite_ref-654" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-654">&#91;647&#93;</a></sup> In 2016, 89&#160;percent of the 7,300 books transferred to the library were in Hebrew.<sup id="cite_ref-655" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-655">&#91;648&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>In 1966, <a href="/wiki/Shmuel_Yosef_Agnon" title="Shmuel Yosef Agnon">Shmuel Yosef Agnon</a> shared the <a href="/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Literature" title="Nobel Prize in Literature">Nobel Prize in Literature</a> with German Jewish author <a href="/wiki/Nelly_Sachs" title="Nelly Sachs">Nelly Sachs</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-656" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-656">&#91;649&#93;</a></sup> Leading Israeli poets have been <a href="/wiki/Yehuda_Amichai" title="Yehuda Amichai">Yehuda Amichai</a>, <a href="/wiki/Nathan_Alterman" title="Nathan Alterman">Nathan Alterman</a>, <a href="/wiki/Leah_Goldberg" title="Leah Goldberg">Leah Goldberg</a>, and <a href="/wiki/Rachel_Bluwstein" title="Rachel Bluwstein">Rachel Bluwstein</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-657" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-657">&#91;650&#93;</a></sup> Internationally famous contemporary Israeli novelists include <a href="/wiki/Amos_Oz" title="Amos Oz">Amos Oz</a>, <a href="/wiki/Etgar_Keret" title="Etgar Keret">Etgar Keret</a> and <a href="/wiki/David_Grossman" title="David Grossman">David Grossman</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-658" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-658">&#91;651&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-659" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-659">&#91;652&#93;</a></sup> The Israeli-Arab satirist <a href="/wiki/Sayed_Kashua" title="Sayed Kashua">Sayed Kashua</a> (who writes in Hebrew) is also internationally known.<sup class="noprint Inline-Template Template-Fact" style="white-space:nowrap;">&#91;<i><a href="/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed" title="Wikipedia:Citation needed"><span title="This claim needs references to reliable sources. (March 2016)">citation needed</span></a></i>&#93;</sup> Israel has also been the home of <a href="/wiki/Emile_Habibi" title="Emile Habibi">Emile Habibi</a>, whose novel <i><a href="/wiki/The_Secret_Life_of_Saeed:_The_Pessoptimist" title="The Secret Life of Saeed: The Pessoptimist">The Secret Life of Saeed: The Pessoptimist</a></i>, and other writings, won him the Israel prize for Arabic literature.<sup id="cite_ref-660" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-660">&#91;653&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-prize_661-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-prize-661">&#91;654&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h3><span class="mw-headline" id="Music_and_dance">Music and dance</span></h3>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main articles: <a href="/wiki/Music_of_Israel" title="Music of Israel">Music of Israel</a> and <a href="/wiki/Dance_in_Israel" title="Dance in Israel">Dance in Israel</a></div>
<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Israel_Philharmonic_Orchestra.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img alt="Several dozen musicians in formal dress, holding their instruments, behind a conductor" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/88/Israel_Philharmonic_Orchestra.jpg/220px-Israel_Philharmonic_Orchestra.jpg" decoding="async" width="220" height="165" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/88/Israel_Philharmonic_Orchestra.jpg/330px-Israel_Philharmonic_Orchestra.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/88/Israel_Philharmonic_Orchestra.jpg/440px-Israel_Philharmonic_Orchestra.jpg 2x" data-file-width="1824" data-file-height="1368" /></a><figcaption><a href="/wiki/Israel_Philharmonic_Orchestra" title="Israel Philharmonic Orchestra">Israel Philharmonic Orchestra</a> conducted by <a href="/wiki/Zubin_Mehta" title="Zubin Mehta">Zubin Mehta</a></figcaption></figure>
<p><a href="/wiki/Music_of_Israel" title="Music of Israel">Israeli music</a> contains musical influences from all over the world; <a href="/wiki/Mizrahi_music" title="Mizrahi music">Mizrahi</a> and <a href="/wiki/Sephardic_music" title="Sephardic music">Sephardic music</a>, <a href="/wiki/Hasidic_Judaism" title="Hasidic Judaism">Hasidic</a> melodies, <a href="/wiki/Greek_music_in_Israel" title="Greek music in Israel">Greek music</a>, <a href="/wiki/Jazz" title="Jazz">jazz</a>, and <a href="/wiki/Pop_rock" title="Pop rock">pop rock</a> are all part of the music scene.<sup id="cite_ref-662" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-662">&#91;655&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-663" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-663">&#91;656&#93;</a></sup> Among Israel's world-renowned<sup id="cite_ref-664" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-664">&#91;657&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-665" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-665">&#91;658&#93;</a></sup> orchestras is the <a href="/wiki/Israel_Philharmonic_Orchestra" title="Israel Philharmonic Orchestra">Israel Philharmonic Orchestra</a>, which has been in operation for over seventy years and today performs more than two hundred concerts each year.<sup id="cite_ref-666" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-666">&#91;659&#93;</a></sup> <a href="/wiki/Itzhak_Perlman" title="Itzhak Perlman">Itzhak Perlman</a>, <a href="/wiki/Pinchas_Zukerman" title="Pinchas Zukerman">Pinchas Zukerman</a> and <a href="/wiki/Ofra_Haza" title="Ofra Haza">Ofra Haza</a> are among the internationally acclaimed musicians born in Israel. <a href="/wiki/Israel_in_the_Eurovision_Song_Contest" title="Israel in the Eurovision Song Contest">Israel has participated</a> in the <a href="/wiki/Eurovision_Song_Contest" title="Eurovision Song Contest">Eurovision Song Contest</a> nearly every year since 1973, winning the competition four times and hosting it twice.<sup id="cite_ref-667" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-667">&#91;660&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-668" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-668">&#91;661&#93;</a></sup> <a href="/wiki/Eilat" title="Eilat">Eilat</a> has hosted its own international music festival, the <a href="/wiki/Red_Sea_Jazz_Festival" title="Red Sea Jazz Festival">Red Sea Jazz Festival</a>, every summer since 1987.<sup id="cite_ref-669" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-669">&#91;662&#93;</a></sup> The nation's canonical <a href="/wiki/Folk_music" title="Folk music">folk songs</a>, known as "Songs of the Land of Israel", deal with the experiences of the pioneers in building the Jewish homeland.<sup id="cite_ref-670" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-670">&#91;663&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h3><span class="mw-headline" id="Cinema_and_theatre">Cinema and theatre</span></h3>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main article: <a href="/wiki/Cinema_of_Israel" title="Cinema of Israel">Cinema of Israel</a></div>
<p>Ten Israeli films <a href="/wiki/List_of_Israeli_submissions_for_the_Academy_Award_for_Best_Foreign_Language_Film" class="mw-redirect" title="List of Israeli submissions for the Academy Award for Best Foreign Language Film">have been final nominees</a> for <a href="/wiki/Academy_Award_for_Best_Foreign_Language_Film" class="mw-redirect" title="Academy Award for Best Foreign Language Film">Best Foreign Language Film</a> at the <a href="/wiki/Academy_Awards" title="Academy Awards">Academy Awards</a> since the establishment of Israel. The 2009 movie <i><a href="/wiki/Ajami_(film)" title="Ajami (film)">Ajami</a></i> was the third consecutive nomination of an Israeli film.<sup id="cite_ref-671" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-671">&#91;664&#93;</a></sup> Palestinian Israeli filmmakers have made a number of films dealing with the Arab-Israeli conflict and the status of Palestinians within Israel, such as <a href="/wiki/Mohammed_Bakri" class="mw-redirect" title="Mohammed Bakri">Mohammed Bakri</a>'s 2002 film <i><a href="/wiki/Jenin,_Jenin" title="Jenin, Jenin">Jenin, Jenin</a></i> and <i><a href="/wiki/The_Syrian_Bride" title="The Syrian Bride">The Syrian Bride</a></i>.<sup class="noprint Inline-Template Template-Fact" style="white-space:nowrap;">&#91;<i><a href="/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed" title="Wikipedia:Citation needed"><span title="This claim needs references to reliable sources. (March 2016)">citation needed</span></a></i>&#93;</sup>
</p><p>Continuing the strong theatrical traditions of the <a href="/wiki/Yiddish_theatre" title="Yiddish theatre">Yiddish theatre</a> in Eastern Europe, Israel maintains a vibrant theatre scene. Founded in 1918, <a href="/wiki/Habima_Theatre" title="Habima Theatre">Habima Theatre</a> in Tel Aviv is Israel's oldest <a href="/wiki/Repertory_theater" class="mw-redirect" title="Repertory theater">repertory theater</a> company and national theater.<sup id="cite_ref-672" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-672">&#91;665&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h3><span class="mw-headline" id="Media">Media</span></h3>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main article: <a href="/wiki/Media_of_Israel" class="mw-redirect" title="Media of Israel">Media of Israel</a></div>
<p>The 2017 <i><a href="/wiki/Freedom_of_the_Press_(report)" title="Freedom of the Press (report)">Freedom of the Press</a></i> annual report by <a href="/wiki/Freedom_House" title="Freedom House">Freedom House</a> ranked Israel as the <a href="/wiki/MENA" class="mw-redirect" title="MENA">Middle East and North Africa</a>'s most free country, and 64th globally.<sup id="cite_ref-673" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-673">&#91;666&#93;</a></sup> In the 2017 <a href="/wiki/Press_Freedom_Index" class="mw-redirect" title="Press Freedom Index">Press Freedom Index</a> by <a href="/wiki/Reporters_Without_Borders" title="Reporters Without Borders">Reporters Without Borders</a>, Israel (including "Israel extraterritorial" since 2013 ranking)<sup id="cite_ref-674" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-674">&#91;667&#93;</a></sup> was placed 91st of 180 countries, first in the Middle East and North Africa region.<sup id="cite_ref-675" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-675">&#91;668&#93;</a></sup> Reporters Without Borders noted that "Palestinian journalists are systematically subjected to violence as a result of their coverage of events in the West Bank".<sup id="cite_ref-676" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-676">&#91;669&#93;</a></sup> More than fifty Palestinian journalists have been killed by Israel since 2001.<sup id="cite_ref-Guyer_2022_677-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Guyer_2022-677">&#91;670&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h3><span class="mw-headline" id="Museums">Museums</span></h3>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">For a more comprehensive list, see <a href="/wiki/List_of_Israeli_museums" title="List of Israeli museums">List of Israeli museums</a>.</div>
<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Billy_Rose_Art_Garden_(14755133799).jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/67/Billy_Rose_Art_Garden_%2814755133799%29.jpg/220px-Billy_Rose_Art_Garden_%2814755133799%29.jpg" decoding="async" width="220" height="142" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/67/Billy_Rose_Art_Garden_%2814755133799%29.jpg/330px-Billy_Rose_Art_Garden_%2814755133799%29.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/67/Billy_Rose_Art_Garden_%2814755133799%29.jpg/440px-Billy_Rose_Art_Garden_%2814755133799%29.jpg 2x" data-file-width="4752" data-file-height="3062" /></a><figcaption><a href="/wiki/Shrine_of_the_Book" title="Shrine of the Book">Shrine of the Book</a>, repository of the <a href="/wiki/Dead_Sea_Scrolls" title="Dead Sea Scrolls">Dead Sea Scrolls</a> in Jerusalem</figcaption></figure>
<p>The <a href="/wiki/Israel_Museum" title="Israel Museum">Israel Museum</a> in Jerusalem is one of Israel's most important cultural institutions<sup id="cite_ref-imj_678-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-imj-678">&#91;671&#93;</a></sup> and houses the <a href="/wiki/Dead_Sea_Scrolls" title="Dead Sea Scrolls">Dead Sea Scrolls</a>,<sup id="cite_ref-679" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-679">&#91;672&#93;</a></sup> along with an extensive collection of <a href="/wiki/Judaica" class="mw-redirect" title="Judaica">Judaica</a> and <a href="/wiki/European_art" class="mw-redirect" title="European art">European art</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-imj_678-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-imj-678">&#91;671&#93;</a></sup> Israel's national <a href="/wiki/The_Holocaust" title="The Holocaust">Holocaust</a> museum, <a href="/wiki/Yad_Vashem" title="Yad Vashem">Yad Vashem</a>, is the world central archive of Holocaust-related information.<sup id="cite_ref-680" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-680">&#91;673&#93;</a></sup> <a href="/wiki/ANU_-_Museum_of_the_Jewish_People" title="ANU - Museum of the Jewish People">ANU - Museum of the Jewish People</a> on the campus of <a href="/wiki/Tel_Aviv_University" title="Tel Aviv University">Tel Aviv University</a>, is an interactive museum devoted to the history of Jewish communities around the world.<sup id="cite_ref-681" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-681">&#91;674&#93;</a></sup> Apart from the major museums in large cities, there are high-quality art spaces in many towns and <a href="/wiki/Kibbutz" title="Kibbutz">kibbutzim</a>. Mishkan LeOmanut in kibbutz <a href="/wiki/Ein_Harod_(Meuhad)" title="Ein Harod (Meuhad)">Ein Harod Meuhad</a> is the largest art museum in the north of the country.<sup id="cite_ref-682" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-682">&#91;675&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Israel has the highest number of museums per capita in the world.<sup id="cite_ref-683" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-683">&#91;676&#93;</a></sup> Several Israeli museums are devoted to Islamic culture, including the <a href="/wiki/Rockefeller_Museum" class="mw-redirect" title="Rockefeller Museum">Rockefeller Museum</a> and the <a href="/wiki/L._A._Mayer_Institute_for_Islamic_Art" class="mw-redirect" title="L. A. Mayer Institute for Islamic Art">L. A. Mayer Institute for Islamic Art</a>, both in Jerusalem. The Rockefeller specializes in archaeological remains from the Ottoman and other periods of Middle East history. It is also the home of the first <a href="/wiki/Hominid" class="mw-redirect" title="Hominid">hominid</a> fossil skull found in Western Asia, called <a href="/wiki/Galilee_Man" class="mw-redirect" title="Galilee Man">Galilee Man</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-684" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-684">&#91;677&#93;</a></sup> A cast of the skull is on display at the Israel Museum.<sup id="cite_ref-685" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-685">&#91;678&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h3><span class="mw-headline" id="Cuisine">Cuisine</span></h3>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main article: <a href="/wiki/Israeli_cuisine" title="Israeli cuisine">Israeli cuisine</a></div>
<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Food_in_Israel.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/8b/Food_in_Israel.jpg/220px-Food_in_Israel.jpg" decoding="async" width="220" height="149" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/8b/Food_in_Israel.jpg/330px-Food_in_Israel.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/8b/Food_in_Israel.jpg/440px-Food_in_Israel.jpg 2x" data-file-width="2390" data-file-height="1620" /></a><figcaption>A meal including <a href="/wiki/Falafel" title="Falafel">falafel</a>, <a href="/wiki/Hummus" title="Hummus">hummus</a>, <a href="/wiki/French_fries" title="French fries">French fries</a> and <a href="/wiki/Israeli_salad" title="Israeli salad">Israeli salad</a></figcaption></figure>
<p><a href="/wiki/Israeli_cuisine" title="Israeli cuisine">Israeli cuisine</a> includes local dishes as well as <a href="/wiki/Jewish_cuisine" title="Jewish cuisine">Jewish cuisine</a> brought to the country by immigrants from the <a href="/wiki/Jewish_diaspora" title="Jewish diaspora">diaspora</a>. Since the establishment of the state in 1948, and particularly since the late 1970s, an Israeli <a href="/wiki/Fusion_cuisine" title="Fusion cuisine">fusion cuisine</a> has developed.<sup id="cite_ref-raviv_686-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-raviv-686">&#91;679&#93;</a></sup> Israeli cuisine has adopted, and continues to adapt, elements of the <a href="/wiki/Cuisine_of_the_Mizrahi_Jews" class="mw-redirect" title="Cuisine of the Mizrahi Jews">Mizrahi</a>, <a href="/wiki/Cuisine_of_the_Sephardic_Jews" class="mw-redirect" title="Cuisine of the Sephardic Jews">Sephardi</a>, and <a href="/wiki/Ashkenazi_cuisine" class="mw-redirect" title="Ashkenazi cuisine">Ashkenazi</a> styles of cooking. It incorporates many foods traditionally eaten in the <a href="/wiki/Levantine_cuisine" title="Levantine cuisine">Levantine</a>, <a href="/wiki/Arab_cuisine" title="Arab cuisine">Arab</a>, <a href="/wiki/Middle_Eastern_cuisine" title="Middle Eastern cuisine">Middle Eastern</a> and <a href="/wiki/Mediterranean_cuisine" title="Mediterranean cuisine">Mediterranean</a> cuisines, such as <a href="/wiki/Falafel" title="Falafel">falafel</a>, <a href="/wiki/Hummus" title="Hummus">hummus</a>, <a href="/wiki/Shakshouka" title="Shakshouka">shakshouka</a>, <a href="/wiki/Couscous" title="Couscous">couscous</a>, and <a href="/wiki/Za%27atar" title="Za&#39;atar">za'atar</a>. <a href="/wiki/Schnitzel" title="Schnitzel">Schnitzel</a>, <a href="/wiki/Pizza" title="Pizza">pizza</a>, <a href="/wiki/Hamburger" title="Hamburger">hamburgers</a>, <a href="/wiki/French_fries" title="French fries">French fries</a>, <a href="/wiki/Rice" title="Rice">rice</a> and <a href="/wiki/Salad" title="Salad">salad</a> are also common in Israel.<sup class="noprint Inline-Template Template-Fact" style="white-space:nowrap;">&#91;<i><a href="/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed" title="Wikipedia:Citation needed"><span title="This claim needs references to reliable sources. (March 2016)">citation needed</span></a></i>&#93;</sup>
</p><p>Roughly half of the Israeli-Jewish population attests to keeping <a href="/wiki/Kosher" class="mw-redirect" title="Kosher">kosher</a> at home.<sup id="cite_ref-687" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-687">&#91;680&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-Bernstein_688-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Bernstein-688">&#91;681&#93;</a></sup> <a href="/wiki/Kosher_restaurant" title="Kosher restaurant">Kosher restaurants</a>, though rare in the 1960s, make up around a quarter of the total as of 2015<sup class="plainlinks noexcerpt noprint asof-tag update" style="display:none;"><a class="external text" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Israel&amp;action=edit">&#91;update&#93;</a></sup>, perhaps reflecting the largely secular values of those who dine out.<sup id="cite_ref-raviv_686-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-raviv-686">&#91;679&#93;</a></sup> Hotel restaurants are much more likely to serve kosher food.<sup id="cite_ref-raviv_686-2" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-raviv-686">&#91;679&#93;</a></sup> The non-kosher retail market was traditionally sparse, but grew rapidly and considerably following <a href="/wiki/1990s_Post-Soviet_aliyah" class="mw-redirect" title="1990s Post-Soviet aliyah">the influx of immigrants from the post-Soviet states</a> during the 1990s.<sup id="cite_ref-bernstein_689-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-bernstein-689">&#91;682&#93;</a></sup> Together with non-kosher fish, rabbits and ostriches, <a href="/wiki/Pork" title="Pork">pork</a>—often called "white meat" in Israel<sup id="cite_ref-bernstein_689-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-bernstein-689">&#91;682&#93;</a></sup>—is produced and consumed, though <a href="/wiki/Religious_restrictions_on_the_consumption_of_pork" title="Religious restrictions on the consumption of pork">it is forbidden</a> by both Judaism and Islam.<sup id="cite_ref-690" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-690">&#91;683&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h3><span class="mw-headline" id="Sports">Sports</span></h3>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main article: <a href="/wiki/Sport_in_Israel" title="Sport in Israel">Sport in Israel</a></div>
<figure class="mw-default-size mw-halign-left" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:%D7%99%D7%A8%D7%95%D7%A7_%D7%A2%D7%95%D7%9C%D7%94.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/0c/%D7%99%D7%A8%D7%95%D7%A7_%D7%A2%D7%95%D7%9C%D7%94.jpg/220px-%D7%99%D7%A8%D7%95%D7%A7_%D7%A2%D7%95%D7%9C%D7%94.jpg" decoding="async" width="220" height="165" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/0c/%D7%99%D7%A8%D7%95%D7%A7_%D7%A2%D7%95%D7%9C%D7%94.jpg/330px-%D7%99%D7%A8%D7%95%D7%A7_%D7%A2%D7%95%D7%9C%D7%94.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/0c/%D7%99%D7%A8%D7%95%D7%A7_%D7%A2%D7%95%D7%9C%D7%94.jpg/440px-%D7%99%D7%A8%D7%95%D7%A7_%D7%A2%D7%95%D7%9C%D7%94.jpg 2x" data-file-width="4000" data-file-height="3000" /></a><figcaption><a href="/wiki/Maccabi_Haifa_F.C." title="Maccabi Haifa F.C.">Maccabi Haifa F.C.</a> fans at <a href="/wiki/Sammy_Ofer_Stadium" title="Sammy Ofer Stadium">Sammy Ofer Stadium</a> in the city of Haifa</figcaption></figure>
<p>The most popular spectator sports in Israel are <a href="/wiki/Association_football" title="Association football">association football</a> and <a href="/wiki/Basketball" title="Basketball">basketball</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-691" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-691">&#91;684&#93;</a></sup> The <a href="/wiki/Israeli_Premier_League" title="Israeli Premier League">Israeli Premier League</a> is the country's premier football league, and the <a href="/wiki/Israeli_Basketball_Premier_League" title="Israeli Basketball Premier League">Israeli Basketball Premier League</a> is the premier basketball league.<sup id="cite_ref-692" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-692">&#91;685&#93;</a></sup> <a href="/wiki/Maccabi_Haifa_F.C." title="Maccabi Haifa F.C.">Maccabi Haifa</a>, <a href="/wiki/Maccabi_Tel_Aviv_F.C." title="Maccabi Tel Aviv F.C.">Maccabi Tel Aviv</a>, <a href="/wiki/Hapoel_Tel_Aviv_F.C." title="Hapoel Tel Aviv F.C.">Hapoel Tel Aviv</a> and <a href="/wiki/Beitar_Jerusalem_F.C." title="Beitar Jerusalem F.C.">Beitar Jerusalem</a> are the largest <a href="/wiki/List_of_football_clubs_in_Israel" title="List of football clubs in Israel">football clubs</a>. Maccabi Tel Aviv, Maccabi Haifa and Hapoel Tel Aviv have competed in the <a href="/wiki/UEFA_Champions_League" title="UEFA Champions League">UEFA Champions League</a> and Hapoel Tel Aviv reached the <a href="/wiki/UEFA_Cup" class="mw-redirect" title="UEFA Cup">UEFA Cup</a> quarter-finals. Israel hosted and won the <a href="/wiki/1964_AFC_Asian_Cup" title="1964 AFC Asian Cup">1964 AFC Asian Cup</a>; in 1970 the <a href="/wiki/Israel_national_football_team" title="Israel national football team">Israel national football team</a> qualified for the <a href="/wiki/1970_FIFA_World_Cup" title="1970 FIFA World Cup">FIFA World Cup</a>, the only time it participated in the World Cup. The <a href="/wiki/1974_Asian_Games" title="1974 Asian Games">1974 Asian Games</a>, held in Tehran, were the last Asian Games in which Israel <a href="/wiki/Israel_at_the_Asian_Games" title="Israel at the Asian Games">participated</a>, plagued by the Arab countries that <a href="/wiki/Boycotts_of_Israel_in_sports" title="Boycotts of Israel in sports">refused</a> to compete with Israel. Israel was excluded from the <a href="/wiki/1978_Asian_Games" title="1978 Asian Games">1978 Asian Games</a> and since then has not competed in Asian sport events.<sup id="cite_ref-693" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-693">&#91;686&#93;</a></sup> In 1994, <a href="/wiki/UEFA" title="UEFA">UEFA</a> agreed to admit Israel, and its football teams now compete in Europe.<sup class="noprint Inline-Template Template-Fact" style="white-space:nowrap;">&#91;<i><a href="/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed" title="Wikipedia:Citation needed"><span title="This claim needs references to reliable sources. (March 2016)">citation needed</span></a></i>&#93;</sup> <a href="/wiki/Maccabi_Tel_Aviv_B.C." title="Maccabi Tel Aviv B.C.">Maccabi Tel Aviv B.C.</a> has won the <a href="/wiki/FIBA_European_Champions_Cup_and_EuroLeague_records_and_statistics" title="FIBA European Champions Cup and EuroLeague records and statistics">European championship</a> in basketball six times.<sup id="cite_ref-694" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-694">&#91;687&#93;</a></sup> In 2016, the country was chosen as a host for the <a href="/wiki/EuroBasket_2017" title="EuroBasket 2017">EuroBasket 2017</a>.
</p><p>Israel has won <a href="/wiki/Israel_at_the_Olympics" title="Israel at the Olympics">nine Olympic medals</a> since its first win <a href="/wiki/1992_Summer_Olympics" title="1992 Summer Olympics">in 1992</a>, including a gold medal in <a href="/wiki/Sailing_at_the_2004_Summer_Olympics_%E2%80%93_Men%27s_Mistral_One_Design" title="Sailing at the 2004 Summer Olympics – Men&#39;s Mistral One Design">windsurfing</a> at the <a href="/wiki/2004_Summer_Olympics" title="2004 Summer Olympics">2004 Summer Olympics</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-695" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-695">&#91;688&#93;</a></sup> Israel has won <a href="/wiki/Israel_at_the_Paralympics" title="Israel at the Paralympics">over 100</a> gold medals in the <a href="/wiki/Paralympic_Games" title="Paralympic Games">Paralympic Games</a> and is ranked 20th in the <a href="/wiki/All-time_Paralympic_Games_medal_table" title="All-time Paralympic Games medal table">all-time medal count</a>. The <a href="/wiki/1968_Summer_Paralympics" title="1968 Summer Paralympics">1968 Summer Paralympics</a> were hosted by Israel.<sup id="cite_ref-696" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-696">&#91;689&#93;</a></sup> The <a href="/wiki/Maccabiah_Games" title="Maccabiah Games">Maccabiah Games</a>, an Olympic-style event for <a href="/wiki/List_of_Jews_in_sports" title="List of Jews in sports">Jewish</a> and Israeli athletes, was inaugurated in the 1930s, and has been held every four years since then. Israeli tennis champion <a href="/wiki/Shahar_Pe%27er" title="Shahar Pe&#39;er">Shahar Pe'er</a> ranked 11th in the world on 31 January 2011.<sup id="cite_ref-697" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-697">&#91;690&#93;</a></sup> <a href="/wiki/Krav_Maga" title="Krav Maga">Krav Maga</a>, a martial art developed by Jewish ghetto defenders during the struggle against <a href="/wiki/Fascism" title="Fascism">fascism</a> in Europe, is used by the Israeli security forces and police. Its effectiveness and practical approach to self-defense, have won it widespread admiration and adherence around the world.<sup id="cite_ref-698" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-698">&#91;691&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:BorisGelfandSicilianDefence.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/89/BorisGelfandSicilianDefence.jpg/220px-BorisGelfandSicilianDefence.jpg" decoding="async" width="220" height="203" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/89/BorisGelfandSicilianDefence.jpg/330px-BorisGelfandSicilianDefence.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/89/BorisGelfandSicilianDefence.jpg/440px-BorisGelfandSicilianDefence.jpg 2x" data-file-width="2943" data-file-height="2722" /></a><figcaption><a href="/wiki/Boris_Gelfand" title="Boris Gelfand">Boris Gelfand</a>, chess <a href="/wiki/Grandmaster_(chess)" title="Grandmaster (chess)">Grandmaster</a></figcaption></figure>
<p><a href="/wiki/Chess" title="Chess">Chess</a> is a leading sport in Israel and is enjoyed by people of all ages. There are many Israeli grandmasters and <a href="/wiki/List_of_Israeli_chess_players" title="List of Israeli chess players">Israeli chess players</a> have won a number of youth world championships.<sup id="cite_ref-699" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-699">&#91;692&#93;</a></sup> Israel stages an annual international <a href="/wiki/Israeli_Chess_Championship" title="Israeli Chess Championship">championship</a> and hosted the <a href="/wiki/World_Team_Chess_Championship" title="World Team Chess Championship">World Team Chess Championship</a> in 2005. The Ministry of Education and the <a href="/wiki/FIDE" title="FIDE">World Chess Federation</a> agreed upon a project of teaching chess within Israeli schools, and it has been introduced into the curriculum of some schools.<sup id="cite_ref-700" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-700">&#91;693&#93;</a></sup> The city of <a href="/wiki/Beersheba" title="Beersheba">Beersheba</a> has become a national chess center, with the game being taught in the city's kindergartens. Owing partly to Soviet immigration, it is home to the largest number of <a href="/wiki/Grandmaster_(chess)" title="Grandmaster (chess)">chess grandmasters</a> of any city in the world.<sup id="cite_ref-701" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-701">&#91;694&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-702" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-702">&#91;695&#93;</a></sup> The Israeli chess team won the silver medal at the <a href="/wiki/38th_Chess_Olympiad" title="38th Chess Olympiad">2008 Chess Olympiad</a><sup id="cite_ref-703" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-703">&#91;696&#93;</a></sup> and the bronze, coming in third among 148 teams, at the <a href="/wiki/39th_Chess_Olympiad" title="39th Chess Olympiad">2010 Olympiad</a>. Israeli grandmaster <a href="/wiki/Boris_Gelfand" title="Boris Gelfand">Boris Gelfand</a> won the <a href="/wiki/Chess_World_Cup_2009" title="Chess World Cup 2009">Chess World Cup 2009</a><sup id="cite_ref-704" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-704">&#91;697&#93;</a></sup> and the <a href="/wiki/World_Chess_Championship_2012#Candidates_tournament" title="World Chess Championship 2012">2011 Candidates Tournament</a> for the right to challenge the world champion. He lost the <a href="/wiki/World_Chess_Championship_2012" title="World Chess Championship 2012">World Chess Championship 2012</a> to reigning world champion <a href="/wiki/Viswanathan_Anand" title="Viswanathan Anand">Anand</a> after a speed-chess tie breaker.
</p>

(February 2023)">better&#160;source&#160;needed</span></a></i>&#93;</sup> In 2018 <a href="/wiki/Basic_Law:_Israel_as_the_Nation-State_of_the_Jewish_People" title="Basic Law: Israel as the Nation-State of the Jewish People">its classification</a> was changed to a 'special status in the state' with its use by state institutions to be set in law.<sup id="cite_ref-lang2_11-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-lang2-11">&#91;9&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-lang3_12-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-lang3-12">&#91;10&#93;</a></sup></span>

<li id="cite_note-oecd-17"><span class="mw-cite-backlink">^ <a href="#cite_ref-oecd_17-0"><sup><i><b>a</b></i></sup></a> <a href="#cite_ref-oecd_17-1"><sup><i><b>b</b></i></sup></a> <a href="#cite_ref-oecd_17-2"><sup><i><b>c</b></i></sup></a> <a href="#cite_ref-oecd_17-3"><sup><i><b>d</b></i></sup></a></span> <span class="reference-text">Israeli population and economic data covers the economic territory of Israel, including the Golan Heights, East Jerusalem and Israeli settlements in the West Bank.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEOECD2011_417-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEOECD2011-417">&#91;410&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-418" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-418">&#91;411&#93;</a></sup></span>
</li>
<li id="cite_note-23"><span class="mw-cite-backlink"><b><a href="#cite_ref-23">^</a></b></span> <span class="reference-text">The <a href="/wiki/Jerusalem_Law" title="Jerusalem Law">Jerusalem Law</a> states that "Jerusalem, complete and united, is the capital of Israel" and the city serves as the seat of the government, home to the President's residence, government offices, supreme court, and <a href="/wiki/Knesset" title="Knesset">parliament</a>. <a href="/wiki/United_Nations_Security_Council_Resolution_478" title="United Nations Security Council Resolution 478">United Nations Security Council Resolution 478</a> (20 August 1980; 14–0, U.S. abstaining) declared the Jerusalem Law "null and void" and called on member states to withdraw their diplomatic missions from Jerusalem (see <a href="#CITEREFKellerman1993">Kellerman 1993</a>, p.&#160;140). See <a href="/wiki/Status_of_Jerusalem" title="Status of Jerusalem">Status of Jerusalem</a> for more information.</span>
</li>
<li id="cite_note-27"><span class="mw-cite-backlink"><b><a href="#cite_ref-27">^</a></b></span> <span class="reference-text">Tens of thousands of Jews in Arab countries left their homes because of the 1948 war as well, pushed by a combination of anti-Semitic feeling and legislation, religious feeling, Zionist activity, economic factors, the end of colonial rule, and other reasons.The decision to leave varied by circumstance, as well as by country and social class. Approximately 260,000 Jews from the Arab world moved to Israel during and immediately after the war.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEFischbach200826–27_26-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFischbach200826–27-26">&#91;21&#93;</a></sup></span>

OUP. <a href="/wiki/ISBN_(identifier)" class="mw-redirect" title="ISBN (identifier)">ISBN</a>&#160;<a href="/wiki/Special:BookSources/978-0-19-518364-1" title="Special:BookSources/978-0-19-518364-1"><bdi>978-0-19-518364-1</bdi></a>.</cite><span title="ctx_ver=Z39.88-2004&amp;rft_val_fmt=info%3Aofi%2Ffmt%3Akev%3Amtx%3Abook&amp;rft.genre=book&amp;rft.btitle=Handbook+to+Life+in+Ancient+Mesopotamia&amp;rft.pub=OUP&amp;rft.date=2005-07-14&amp;rft.isbn=978-0-19-518364-1&amp;rft.aulast=Bertman&amp;rft.aufirst=Stephen&amp;rft_id=https%3A%2F%2Fbooks.google.com%2Fbooks%3Fid%3D1C4NKp4zgIQC%26q%3Debla%2520israel%2520ishmael%2520abraham%26pg%3DPA317&amp;rfr_id=info%3Asid%2Fen.wikipedia.org%3AIsrael" class="Z3988"></span> and <link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1133582631"><cite id="CITEREFMeindert_Dijkstra2010" class="citation book cs1">Meindert Dijkstra (2010). "Origins of Israel between history and ideology". In <a href="/wiki/Lester_L._Grabbe" title="Lester L. Grabbe">Becking, Bob</a>; Grabbe, Lester (eds.). <i>Between Evidence and Ideology Essays on the History of Ancient Israel read at the Joint Meeting of the Society for Old Testament Study and the Oud Testamentisch Werkgezelschap Lincoln, July 2009</i>. Brill. p.&#160;47. <a href="/wiki/ISBN_(identifier)" class="mw-redirect" title="ISBN (identifier)">ISBN</a>&#160;<a href="/wiki/Special:BookSources/978-90-04-18737-5" title="Special:BookSources/978-90-04-18737-5"><bdi>978-90-04-18737-5</bdi></a>. <q>As a West Semitic personal name it existed long before it became a tribal or a geographical name. This is not without significance, though is it rarely mentioned. We learn of a maryanu named ysr"il (*Yi¡sr—a"ilu) from Ugarit living in the same period, but the name was already used a thousand years before in Ebla. The word Israel originated as a West Semitic personal name. One of the many names that developed into the name of the ancestor of a clan, of a tribe and finally of a people and a nation.</q></cite><span title="ctx_ver=Z39.88-2004&amp;rft_val_fmt=info%3Aofi%2Ffmt%3Akev%3Amtx%3Abook&amp;rft.genre=bookitem&amp;rft.atitle=Origins+of+Israel+between+history+and+ideology&amp;rft.btitle=Between+Evidence+and+Ideology+Essays+on+the+History+of+Ancient+Israel+read+at+the+Joint+Meeting+of+the+Society+for+Old+Testament+Study+and+the+Oud+Testamentisch+Werkgezelschap+Lincoln%2C+July+2009&amp;rft.pages=47&amp;rft.pub=Brill&amp;rft.date=2010&amp;rft.isbn=978-90-04-18737-5&amp;rft.au=Meindert+Dijkstra&amp;rfr_id=info%3Asid%2Fen.wikipedia.org%3AIsrael" class="Z3988"></span></span>

<li id="cite_note-59"><span class="mw-cite-backlink"><b><a href="#cite_ref-59">^</a></b></span> <span class="reference-text">Mark Smith in "The Early History of God: Yahweh and Other Deities of Ancient Israel" states "Despite the long regnant model that the Canaanites and Israelites were people of fundamentally different culture, archaeological data now casts doubt on this view. The material culture of the region exhibits numerous common points between Israelites and Canaanites in the Iron I period (c. 1200–1000&#160;BCE). The record would suggest that the Israelite culture largely overlapped with and derived from Canaanite culture... In short, Israelite culture was largely Canaanite in nature. Given the information available, one cannot maintain a radical cultural separation between Canaanites and Israelites for the Iron I period." (pp. 6–7). Smith, Mark (2002) "The Early History of God: Yahweh and Other Deities of Ancient Israel" (Eerdman's)</span>

<li id="cite_note-88"><span class="mw-cite-backlink"><b><a href="#cite_ref-88">^</a></b></span> <span class="reference-text"><link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1133582631"><cite id="CITEREFHelyerMcDonald2013" class="citation book cs1">Helyer, Larry R.; McDonald, Lee Martin (2013). "The Hasmoneans and the Hasmonean Era". In Green, Joel B.; McDonald, Lee Martin (eds.). <i>The World of the New Testament: Cultural, Social, and Historical Contexts</i>. Baker Academic. pp.&#160;45–47. <a href="/wiki/ISBN_(identifier)" class="mw-redirect" title="ISBN (identifier)">ISBN</a>&#160;<a href="/wiki/Special:BookSources/978-0-8010-9861-1" title="Special:BookSources/978-0-8010-9861-1"><bdi>978-0-8010-9861-1</bdi></a>. <a href="/wiki/OCLC_(identifier)" class="mw-redirect" title="OCLC (identifier)">OCLC</a>&#160;<a rel="nofollow" class="external text" href="https://www.worldcat.org/oclc/961153992">961153992</a>. <q>The ensuing power struggle left Hyrcanus with a free hand in Judea, and he quickly reasserted Jewish sovereignty... Hyrcanus then engaged in a series of military campaigns aimed at territorial expansion. He first conquered areas in the Transjordan. He then turned his attention to Samaria, which had long separated Judea from the northern Jewish settlements in Lower Galilee. In the south, Adora and Marisa were conquered; (Aristobulus') primary accomplishment was annexing and Judaizing the region of Iturea, located between the Lebanon and Anti-Lebanon mountains</q></cite><span title="ctx_ver=Z39.88-2004&amp;rft_val_fmt=info%3Aofi%2Ffmt%3Akev%3Amtx%3Abook&amp;rft.genre=bookitem&amp;rft.atitle=The+Hasmoneans+and+the+Hasmonean+Era&amp;rft.btitle=The+World+of+the+New+Testament%3A+Cultural%2C+Social%2C+and+Historical+Contexts&amp;rft.pages=45-47&amp;rft.pub=Baker+Academic&amp;rft.date=2013&amp;rft_id=info%3Aoclcnum%2F961153992&amp;rft.isbn=978-0-8010-9861-1&amp;rft.aulast=Helyer&amp;rft.aufirst=Larry+R.&amp;rft.au=McDonald%2C+Lee+Martin&amp;rfr_id=info%3Asid%2Fen.wikipedia.org%3AIsrael" class="Z3988"></span></span>

<li id="cite_note-89"><span class="mw-cite-backlink"><b><a href="#cite_ref-89">^</a></b></span> <span class="reference-text"><link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1133582631"><cite id="CITEREFBen-Sasson1976" class="citation book cs1">Ben-Sasson, H.H. (1976). <i>A History of the Jewish People</i>. Harvard University Press. p.&#160;226. <a href="/wiki/ISBN_(identifier)" class="mw-redirect" title="ISBN (identifier)">ISBN</a>&#160;<a href="/wiki/Special:BookSources/978-0-674-39731-6" title="Special:BookSources/978-0-674-39731-6"><bdi>978-0-674-39731-6</bdi></a>. <q>The expansion of Hasmonean Judea took place gradually. Under Jonathan, Judea annexed southern Samaria and began to expand in the direction of the coast plain... The main ethnic changes were the work of John Hyrcanus... it was in his days and those of his son Aristobulus that the annexation of Idumea, Samaria and Galilee and the consolidation of Jewish settlement in Trans-Jordan was completed. Alexander Jannai, continuing the work of his predecessors, expanded Judean rule to the entire coastal plain, from the Carmel to the Egyptian border... and to additional areas in Trans-Jordan, including some of the Greek cities there.</q></cite><span title="ctx_ver=Z39.88-2004&amp;rft_val_fmt=info%3Aofi%2Ffmt%3Akev%3Amtx%3Abook&amp;rft.genre=book&amp;rft.btitle=A+History+of+the+Jewish+People&amp;rft.pages=226&amp;rft.pub=Harvard+University+Press&amp;rft.date=1976&amp;rft.isbn=978-0-674-39731-6&amp;rft.aulast=Ben-Sasson&amp;rft.aufirst=H.H.&amp;rfr_id=info%3Asid%2Fen.wikipedia.org%3AIsrael" class="Z3988"></span></span>

<li id="cite_note-90"><span class="mw-cite-backlink"><b><a href="#cite_ref-90">^</a></b></span> <span class="reference-text"><link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1133582631"><cite id="CITEREFBen-Eliyahu2019" class="citation book cs1">Ben-Eliyahu, Eyal (30 April 2019). <i>Identity and Territory: Jewish Perceptions of Space in Antiquity</i>. Univ of California Press. p.&#160;13. <a href="/wiki/ISBN_(identifier)" class="mw-redirect" title="ISBN (identifier)">ISBN</a>&#160;<a href="/wiki/Special:BookSources/978-0-520-29360-1" title="Special:BookSources/978-0-520-29360-1"><bdi>978-0-520-29360-1</bdi></a>. <a href="/wiki/OCLC_(identifier)" class="mw-redirect" title="OCLC (identifier)">OCLC</a>&#160;<a rel="nofollow" class="external text" href="https://www.worldcat.org/oclc/1103519319">1103519319</a>. <q>From the beginning of the Second Temple period until the Muslim conquest—the land was part of imperial space. This was true from the early Persian period, as well as the time of Ptolemy and the Seleucids. The only exception was the Hasmonean Kingdom, with its sovereign Jewish rule—first over Judah and later, in Alexander Jannaeus's prime, extending to the coast, the north, and the eastern banks of the Jordan.</q></cite><span title="ctx_ver=Z39.88-2004&amp;rft_val_fmt=info%3Aofi%2Ffmt%3Akev%3Amtx%3Abook&amp;rft.genre=book&amp;rft.btitle=Identity+and+Territory%3A+Jewish+Perceptions+of+Space+in+Antiquity&amp;rft.pages=13&amp;rft.pub=Univ+of+California+Press&amp;rft.date=2019-04-30&amp;rft_id=info%3Aoclcnum%2F1103519319&amp;rft.isbn=978-0-520-29360-1&amp;rft.aulast=Ben-Eliyahu&amp;rft.aufirst=Eyal&amp;rfr_id=info%3Asid%2Fen.wikipedia.org%3AIsrael" class="Z3988"></span></span>

<li id="cite_note-:8-91"><span class="mw-cite-backlink">^ <a href="#cite_ref-:8_91-0"><sup><i><b>a</b></i></sup></a> <a href="#cite_ref-:8_91-1"><sup><i><b>b</b></i></sup></a></span> <span class="reference-text"><link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1133582631"><cite id="CITEREFSchwartz2014" class="citation book cs1">Schwartz, Seth (2014). <i>The ancient Jews from Alexander to Muhammad</i>. Cambridge. pp.&#160;85–86. <a href="/wiki/ISBN_(identifier)" class="mw-redirect" title="ISBN (identifier)">ISBN</a>&#160;<a href="/wiki/Special:BookSources/978-1-107-04127-1" title="Special:BookSources/978-1-107-04127-1"><bdi>978-1-107-04127-1</bdi></a>. <a href="/wiki/OCLC_(identifier)" class="mw-redirect" title="OCLC (identifier)">OCLC</a>&#160;<a rel="nofollow" class="external text" href="https://www.worldcat.org/oclc/863044259">863044259</a>. <q>The year 70 ce marked transformations in demography, politics, Jewish civic status, Palestinian and more general Jewish economic and social structures, Jewish religious life beyond the sacrificial cult, and even Roman politics and the topography of the city of Rome itself. [...] The Revolt's failure had, to begin with, a demographic impact on the Jews of Palestine; many died in battle and as a result of siege conditions, not only in Jerusalem. [...] As indicated above, the figures for captives are conceivably more reliable. If 97,000 is roughly correct as a total for the war, it would mean that a huge percentage of the population was removed from the country, or at the very least displaced from their homes. Nevertheless, only sixty years later, there was a large enough population in the Judaean countryside to stage a massively disruptive second rebellion; this one appears to have ended, in 135, with devastation and depopulation of the district.</q></cite><span title="ctx_ver=Z39.88-2004&amp;rft_val_fmt=info%3Aofi%2Ffmt%3Akev%3Amtx%3Abook&amp;rft.genre=book&amp;rft.btitle=The+ancient+Jews+from+Alexander+to+Muhammad&amp;rft.place=Cambridge&amp;rft.pages=85-86&amp;rft.date=2014&amp;rft_id=info%3Aoclcnum%2F863044259&amp;rft.isbn=978-1-107-04127-1&amp;rft.aulast=Schwartz&amp;rft.aufirst=Seth&amp;rfr_id=info%3Asid%2Fen.wikipedia.org%3AIsrael" class="Z3988"></span><span class="cs1-maint citation-comment"><code class="cs1-code">{{<a href="/wiki/Template:Cite_book" title="Template:Cite book">cite book</a>}}</code>:  CS1 maint: location missing publisher (<a href="/wiki/Category:CS1_maint:_location_missing_publisher" title="Category:CS1 maint: location missing publisher">link</a>)</span></span>

<li id="cite_note-93"><span class="mw-cite-backlink"><b><a href="#cite_ref-93">^</a></b></span> <span class="reference-text"><link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1133582631"><cite id="CITEREFRavivBen_David2021" class="citation journal cs1">Raviv, Dvir; Ben David, Chaim (2021). <a rel="nofollow" class="external text" href="https://doi.org/10.1017%2FS1047759421000271">"Cassius Dio's figures for the demographic consequences of the Bar Kokhba War: Exaggeration or reliable account?"</a>. <i>Journal of Roman Archaeology</i>. <b>34</b> (2): 585–607. <a href="/wiki/Doi_(identifier)" class="mw-redirect" title="Doi (identifier)">doi</a>:<span class="cs1-lock-free" title="Freely accessible"><a rel="nofollow" class="external text" href="https://doi.org/10.1017%2FS1047759421000271">10.1017/S1047759421000271</a></span>. <a href="/wiki/ISSN_(identifier)" class="mw-redirect" title="ISSN (identifier)">ISSN</a>&#160;<a rel="nofollow" class="external text" href="https://www.worldcat.org/issn/1047-7594">1047-7594</a>. <a href="/wiki/S2CID_(identifier)" class="mw-redirect" title="S2CID (identifier)">S2CID</a>&#160;<a rel="nofollow" class="external text" href="https://api.semanticscholar.org/CorpusID:245512193">245512193</a>. <q>Scholars have long doubted the historical accuracy of Cassius Dio's account of the consequences of the Bar Kokhba War (Roman History 69.14). According to this text, considered the most reliable literary source for the Second Jewish Revolt, the war encompassed all of Judea: the Romans destroyed 985 villages and 50 fortresses, and killed 580,000 rebels. This article reassesses Cassius Dio's figures by drawing on new evidence from excavations and surveys in Judea, Transjordan, and the Galilee. Three research methods are combined: an ethno-archaeological comparison with the settlement picture in the Ottoman Period, comparison with similar settlement studies in the Galilee, and an evaluation of settled sites from the Middle Roman Period (70–136CE). The study demonstrates the potential contribution of the archaeological record to this issue and supports the view of Cassius Dio's demographic data as a reliable account, which he based on contemporaneous documentation.</q></cite><span title="ctx_ver=Z39.88-2004&amp;rft_val_fmt=info%3Aofi%2Ffmt%3Akev%3Amtx%3Ajournal&amp;rft.genre=article&amp;rft.jtitle=Journal+of+Roman+Archaeology&amp;rft.atitle=Cassius+Dio%27s+figures+for+the+demographic+consequences+of+the+Bar+Kokhba+War%3A+Exaggeration+or+reliable+account%3F&amp;rft.volume=34&amp;rft.issue=2&amp;rft.pages=585-607&amp;rft.date=2021&amp;rft_id=https%3A%2F%2Fapi.semanticscholar.org%2FCorpusID%3A245512193%23id-name%3DS2CID&amp;rft.issn=1047-7594&amp;rft_id=info%3Adoi%2F10.1017%2FS1047759421000271&amp;rft.aulast=Raviv&amp;rft.aufirst=Dvir&amp;rft.au=Ben+David%2C+Chaim&amp;rft_id=https%3A%2F%2Fdoi.org%2F10.1017%252FS1047759421000271&amp;rfr_id=info%3Asid%2Fen.wikipedia.org%3AIsrael" class="Z3988"></span></span>
</li>
<li id="cite_note-:02-94"><span class="mw-cite-backlink">^ <a href="#cite_ref-:02_94-0"><sup><i><b>a</b></i></sup></a> <a href="#cite_ref-:02_94-1"><sup><i><b>b</b></i></sup></a> <a href="#cite_ref-:02_94-2"><sup><i><b>c</b></i></sup></a></span> <span class="reference-text"><link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1133582631"><cite id="CITEREFMor2016" class="citation book cs1">Mor, Menahem (18 April 2016). <i>The Second Jewish Revolt</i>. BRILL. pp.&#160;483–484. <a href="/wiki/Doi_(identifier)" class="mw-redirect" title="Doi (identifier)">doi</a>:<a rel="nofollow" class="external text" href="https://doi.org/10.1163%2F9789004314634">10.1163/9789004314634</a>. <a href="/wiki/ISBN_(identifier)" class="mw-redirect" title="ISBN (identifier)">ISBN</a>&#160;<a href="/wiki/Special:BookSources/978-90-04-31463-4" title="Special:BookSources/978-90-04-31463-4"><bdi>978-90-04-31463-4</bdi></a>. <q>Land confiscation in Judaea was part of the suppression of the revolt policy of the Romans and punishment for the rebels. But the very claim that the sikarikon laws were annulled for settlement purposes seems to indicate that Jews continued to reside in Judaea even after the Second Revolt. There is no doubt that this area suffered the severest damage from the suppression of the revolt. Settlements in Judaea, such as Herodion and Bethar, had already been destroyed during the course of the revolt, and Jews were expelled from the districts of Gophna, Herodion, and Aqraba. However, it should not be claimed that the region of Judaea was completely destroyed. Jews continued to live in areas such as Lod (Lydda), south of the Hebron Mountain, and the coastal regions. In other areas of the Land of Israel that did not have any direct connection with the Second Revolt, no settlement changes can be identified as resulting from it.</q></cite><span title="ctx_ver=Z39.88-2004&amp;rft_val_fmt=info%3Aofi%2Ffmt%3Akev%3Amtx%3Abook&amp;rft.genre=book&amp;rft.btitle=The+Second+Jewish+Revolt&amp;rft.pages=483-484&amp;rft.pub=BRILL&amp;rft.date=2016-04-18&amp;rft_id=info%3Adoi%2F10.1163%2F9789004314634&amp;rft.isbn=978-90-04-31463-4&amp;rft.aulast=Mor&amp;rft.aufirst=Menahem&amp;rfr_id=info%3Asid%2Fen.wikipedia.org%3AIsrael" class="Z3988"></span></span>

<li id="cite_note-:1-105"><span class="mw-cite-backlink"><b><a href="#cite_ref-:1_105-0">^</a></b></span> <span class="reference-text"><link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1133582631"><cite id="CITEREFEhrlich2022" class="citation book cs1">Ehrlich, Michael (2022). <i>The Islamization of the Holy Land, 634–1800</i>. Leeds, UK: Arc Humanities Press. pp.&#160;3–4. <a href="/wiki/ISBN_(identifier)" class="mw-redirect" title="ISBN (identifier)">ISBN</a>&#160;<a href="/wiki/Special:BookSources/978-1-64189-222-3" title="Special:BookSources/978-1-64189-222-3"><bdi>978-1-64189-222-3</bdi></a>. <a href="/wiki/OCLC_(identifier)" class="mw-redirect" title="OCLC (identifier)">OCLC</a>&#160;<a rel="nofollow" class="external text" href="https://www.worldcat.org/oclc/1302180905">1302180905</a>. <q>The Jewish community strove to recover from the catastrophic results of the Bar Kokhva revolt (132–135 CE). Although some of these attempts were relatively successful, the Jews never fully recovered. During the Late Roman and Byzantine periods, many Jews emigrated to thriving centres in the diaspora, especially Iraq, whereas some converted to Christianity and others continued to live in the Holy Land, especially in Galilee and the coastal plain. During the Byzantine period, the three provinces of Palestine included more than thirty cities, namely, settlements with a bishop see. After the Muslim conquest in the 630s, most of these cities declined and eventually disappeared. As a result, in many cases the local ecclesiastical administration weakened, while in others it simply ceased to exist. Consequently, many local Christians converted to Islam. Thus, almost twelve centuries later, when the army led by Napoleon Bonaparte arrived in the Holy Land, most of the local population was Muslim.</q></cite><span title="ctx_ver=Z39.88-2004&amp;rft_val_fmt=info%3Aofi%2Ffmt%3Akev%3Amtx%3Abook&amp;rft.genre=book&amp;rft.btitle=The+Islamization+of+the+Holy+Land%2C+634%E2%80%931800&amp;rft.place=Leeds%2C+UK&amp;rft.pages=3-4&amp;rft.pub=Arc+Humanities+Press&amp;rft.date=2022&amp;rft_id=info%3Aoclcnum%2F1302180905&amp;rft.isbn=978-1-64189-222-3&amp;rft.aulast=Ehrlich&amp;rft.aufirst=Michael&amp;rfr_id=info%3Asid%2Fen.wikipedia.org%3AIsrael" class="Z3988"></span></span>
